sourceStatement: Ardā Wirāz Nāmag, from The Book of Arda Viraf: the Pahlavi text prepared by Destur Hoshangji Jamaspji Asa, revised and collated with further manuscripts by Martin Haug, assisted by E. W. West (Bombay and London, 1872), {cite}, read from the Internet Archive scan (bookofardaviraf00haug). The § numbers are chapter and sentence in Haug's numbering; later editions divide the chapters differently. Book Pahlavi script has no computer encoding of its own, so the script on the page is Haug's 1872 Pahlavi type itself, cut into words from the scan. Under it are the words as they were read aloud, in D. N. MacKenzie's transcription (the scholarly standard since 1971); the "As written" switch changes that line to the letters of the script in the usual transliteration, Aramaic word-signs in capitals. The print's sentence numbers and punctuation rings are left out of the images. The text is Haug's. Where his reading of a word has since been given up, the word is read as it is today and the note says so; where later editors correct the manuscripts, Haug's print is kept and the note gives the correction. Pronunciation: Middle Persian of the third century as MacKenzie reconstructs it. The translation is new, made from the Pahlavi. Still to do: the "As written" letters were set down from Haug's printed Pahlavi with the help of his own Roman reading of each word, and not every letter has yet been checked against the page.
about: The Book of the Righteous Wirāz is the Zoroastrian journey through heaven and hell, often called the Persian Divine Comedy. It was written in Middle Persian (Pahlavi) and took its present form in the ninth or tenth century, from older material. In a time of doubt the priests choose Wirāz to visit the other world and learn whether their rites reach the gods. He drinks wine and mang, his soul leaves his body for seven days, and guided by Srōš and the god Ādur he crosses the Činwad bridge, sees the rewards of the blessed in the heavens and the punishments of the damned in hell, and is sent back by Ohrmazd to tell the living what he saw.
